choices.explanation: Passage B was a little more detached, as it spent most of the time dispassionately presenting Ayer's ideas. Passage A had more of a point of view.

choices.text: dismissive
choices.explanation: Dismissive is a really strong tone --- I'm not even gonna *listen*, I'm so dismissive. Neither author displayed that extreme tone.

choices.text: detached
choices.explanation:
Other than the last sentence, the author of Passage B was just second-hand information, presenting Ayer's ideas as the foreground.

The author of Passage A was more engaged, using 2nd person pronouns, calling us self-delusional, and recommending the end of retributivist sentencing.

choices.text: ironic
choices.explanation: It's pretty funny to think LSAT would test irony, when it's famously hard to pin down. Passage B is more scholarly and neutral. Passage A has more zazz, more personality, more of an editorial style, so if anything we'd expect to find snark and irony in Passage A.

choices.text: skeptical
choices.explanation:
Both authors are pretty accepting of neuroscience's findings, and they're musing over the implications of them.

*Skeptical* implies "dubious, somewhat unbelieving". Neither author had an un-believing attitude towards anything. If anything, we could say that Passage A was *skeptical* that punishing people for crimes was the right call.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following arguments is most analogous to the argument advanced in passage A?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The argument in A sort of boils down to this, "Since people aren't in control of their actions, they don't really make moral choices. If there's no such thing as bad people making evil decisions, then why are we punishing people? Let's just focus on preventing future harm."

It's almost like dealing with babies or dogs -- sometimes, what's the point in yelling at them? They won't understand what they did wrong. They can't help themselves. Just don't put them in a position to screw up next time.

choices.text: Many word processors are packed with nonessential features that only confuse most users and get in the way of important functions. Word processors with fewer features thus enhance productivity.
choices.explanation: This doesn't seem to have anything to do with "Since they can't be blamed for stuff beyond their control, let's just prevent future harm."

choices.text: Economic models generally presume that actors in an economy are entirely rational. But psychological studies have documented many ways in which people make irrational choices. Thus, economic models, in theory, should not be able to predict human behavior.
choices.tag: Buzzword Bait: rational / Bad Conclusion Match
choices.explanation:
Economic models presume rationality just like legal models presume rationality which makes this tempting.

But this conclusion says that economic models shouldn't predict human behavior. Is Passage A's conclusion saying that legal models shouldn't predict human behavior?

No, it's saying we shouldn't punish people for their behavior, and we ****should**** try to predict future harm (to try to prevent it).

choices.text: The existing program for teaching mathematics in elementary schools is based on mistaken notions about what sorts of mathematical concepts children can grasp, and it should therefore be replaced.
choices.explanation:
It's important to stay very flexible with Analogy questions since it's so hard to predict in advance the type of relationship they will be testing.

This math program is based on mistaken notions about what students can grasp, just like the legal philosophy of retribution is based on mistaken notions about what crime is (it's just involuntary action, not freely chosen mischief by a bad person).

The conclusion of this argument is to get rid of the math program. The conclusion of Passage A was to get rid of the retribution / punishment program we use on law breakers.

choices.text: Civil disobedience is justified only in those cases in which civil law conflicts with one's sincere moral or religious convictions. Any attempt to justify civil disobedience on something other than moral or religious grounds is therefore illegitimate.
choices.explanation:
The argument here is, "Because action X should only be undertaken for reason Y, trying to justify it with any other reason is illegitimate."

I don't know how to match any part of that up with Passage A's argument.

choices.text: Being autonomous does not imply having full control over one's behavior. After all, addicted smokers are unable to exercise control over some behaviors but are nevertheless autonomous in the general sense.
choices.tag: Bad Conclusion Match / Buzzword Bait: control
choices.explanation:
The word control makes this tempting because it's the same topic as the thing we're trying to match. But this is typically a trap, so always investigate with a skeptical eye.

This conclusion is that "X does not imply Y".

The conclusion of passage A was "we should stop doing X and instead do Y".

passages.title: The “Mexican American Generation”
passages.text:
*This passage is adapted from a review of a 1991 book.*

In a recent study, Mario García argues that in the United States between 1930 and 1960 the group of political activists he calls the “Mexican American Generation” was more radical and politically diverse than earlier historians have recognized. Through analysis of the work of some of the era’s most important scholars, García does provide persuasive evidence that in the 1930s and 1940s these activists anticipated many of the reforms proposed by the more militant Chicanos of the 1960s and 1970s. His study, however, suffers from two flaws.

First, García’s analysis of the evidence he provides to demonstrate the Mexican American Generation’s political diversity is not entirely consistent. Indeed, he undermines his primary thesis by emphasizing an underlying consensus among various groups that tends to conceal the full significance of their differences. Groups such as the League of United Latin American Citizens, an organization that encouraged Mexican Americans to pursue a civil rights strategy of assimilation into the United States political and cultural mainstream, were often diametrically opposed to organizations such as the Congress of Spanish- Speaking People, a coalition group that advocated bilingual education and equal rights for resident aliens in the United States. García acknowledges these differences but dismisses them as insignificant, given that the goals of groups as disparate as these centered on liberal reform, not revolution. But one need only note the fierce controversies that occurred during the period over United States immigration policies and the question of assimilation versus cultural maintenance to recognize that Mexican American political history since 1930 has been characterized not by consensus but by intense and lively debate.

Second, García may be exaggerating the degree to which the views of these activists were representative of the ethnic Mexican population residing in the United States during this period. Noting that by 1930 the proportion of the Mexican American population that had been born in the United States had significantly increased, García argues that between 1930 and 1960 a new generation of Mexican American leaders appeared, one that was more acculturated and hence more politically active than its predecessor. Influenced by their experience of discrimination and by the inclusive rhetoric of World War II slogans, these leaders, according to García, were determined to achieve full civil rights for all United States residents of Mexican descent. However, it is not clear how far this outlook extended beyond these activists. Without a better understanding of the political implications of important variables such as patterns of bilingualism and rates of Mexican immigration and naturalization, and the variations in ethnic consciousness these variables help to create, one cannot assume that an increase in the proportion of Mexican Americans born in the United States necessarily resulted in an increase in the ethnic Mexican population’s political activism.

summaries.standard:
****Topic****

Garcia's study

****Framework****

Challenge a Position

****Main Point****

Garcia's study is cool but suffers from two flaws: it semi-contradicts itself when arguing about the diversity of views among the Mexican American activists, and it possibly assumes that the political consciousness of the activists was more widespread among the rest of the Mexican American ethnic population than it really was.

****Summary****

*P1 - Intro of Garcia's book, a compliment, a critiquing thesis*

The author establishes what the thesis of Garcia's book is and drops a little complimentary juice by saying that Garcia does provide "persuasive evidence "that the Mexican American activists in the 30s-60s were important harbingers of more famous activism that occurred in the 60s.

But we get our ****Purpose Pivot**** (but, yet, ****however,**** recently) in the final sentence. We can tell this sentence is the author's thesis because it says that Garcia's study suffers from two flaws, and then we can see that paragraphs 2 and 3 are just unpacking that thesis.

*P2 - First flaw ... support for 'diversity' undermines itself*

The author is basically just saying that Garcia did himself a disservice by acknowledging how much common ground there was among the Mexican American activists of the 30s to 60s, given that Garcia's main point was to convey the diversity of thought within this group (and given that there definitely WAS a lot of diversity within this group).

This is a weird complaint, because it's not the author disagreeing with the content of Garcia's thesis; she's just complaining that he did a poor job in executing his supporting evidence, since he emphasized togetherness, at the expense of better communicating diversity.

*P3 - Second flaw - author thinks activists were an unrepresentative sample*

Here, the author is basically saying that Garcia may go too far in thinking that the political engagement of the activists somehow reflected broader trends among the Mexican American population, when the author feels like most of the regular Mexican Americans were still pretty culturally conservative and shut-off from mainstream American politics.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, the League of United Latin American Citizens differed from the Congress of Spanish-Speaking People in that the League of United Latin American Citizens

choices.text: sought the political goals most popular with other United States citizens
fought for equal rights for resident aliens in the United States
favored a more liberal United States immigration policy
encouraged Mexican Americans to speak Spanish rather than English
encouraged Mexican Americans to adopt the culture of the United States

questions.prompt: It can be inferred from the passage that García would most probably agree with which one of the following statements about the Mexican American political activists of the 1930s and 1940s?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
The best support sentence that contains the keywords "Garcia / 1930s / 1940s" is found in the first paragraph's second to last sentence:

***Garcia** does provide persuasive evidence that in the **1930s** and **1940s** these activists anticipated many of the reforms proposed by the more militant Chicanos of the 1960s and 1970s.*

So from this sentence we can infer that Garcia would probably say that the reforms proposed by or agitated for by Mexican American activists in the 30s/40s foreshadowed ones proposed in the 60s/70s.

There is also a reference in the 3rd paragraph to Garcia's argument that between 1930 and 1960, a new generation of Mexican American leaders appeared, that were more acculturated and politically active than previous generations. So the correct answer could possibly refer to this, but it would be weird for the question stem to advertise 30s/40s when this support sentence is about 1930-1960.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Let's look for something that reinforces our Support Window at the end of the first paragraph.

choices.text: Some of their concerns were similar to those of the Mexican American activists of the 1960s and 1970s.
choices.explanation:
This maps pretty closely to our Support Sentence. And the language, "Some", is deliciously soft.

We were told that
*these activists anticipated many of the reforms proposed by the more militant Chicanos of the 1960s and 1970s.*

That means that the reforms they were proposing were similar (harbingers / foreshadowing / forerunners) of the stuff being proposed in the 60s/70s.

Hence, they had some similar concerns with activists from the 60s/70s.

choices.text: They were more politically diverse than the Mexican American activists of the 1960s and 1970s.
choices.explanation:
In the 2nd paragraph, the author stresses the political (and combative) diversity of thought within the Mexican American activist movement.

*Garcia acknowledges these differences but dismisses them as insignificant*.

So Garcia is actually downplaying the political differences. Most importantly, neither the author nor Garcia compare the political diversity of the 30s/40s to that of the 60s/70s.

choices.text: They were as militant as the Mexican American activists of the 1960s and 1970s.
choices.explanation: Our support sentence towards the end of the 1st paragraph says that the activists of the 60s/70s were **more** militant.

choices.text: Most of them advocated bilingual education and equal rights for resident aliens in the United States.
choices.explanation:
This language about bilingual education / equal rights isn't anywhere near our Support Window.

And answers that use "most" or its synonyms are famously dangerous. We can only pick these if we find support text that talks about "most activists in the 30s/40s" or that generalizes about them in a way that we can assume thereby applies to most.

The concepts of "bilingual education and equal rights for resident aliens" come from the 2nd paragraph. It should unnerve us that this answer is copying that much text verbatim from the passage (that's the hallmark of trap answers, not correct ones).

We are told that "the Congress of Spanish-Speaking people" advocates these two things. We're never told that most Mexican American activists in the 30s/40s do.

choices.text: Most of them were more interested in revolution than in liberal reform.
choices.tag: Too Strong: most / Contradicted, if anything
choices.explanation:
We're told that the activists of the 60s/70s are the more militant ones, so *they* would be the ones more interested in revolution.

And Garcia notes in the 2nd paragraph,
*the goals of groups as disparate as these (different groups of Mexican American activists) centered on liberal reform, not revolution.*

questions.prompt: The passage suggests that García assumes which one of the following to have been true of Mexican Americans between 1930 and 1960?

explanationBlocks.heading: Support Window
explanationBlocks.body:
Does the passage ever say that Garcia assumes something? If we're doing Flex, we can CTRL / Command + F the word "assume".

We'd be taken to the final sentence of the passage, in which the author is rebutting Garcia by saying that,
*one cannot* *****assume***** *that an increase in the proportion of Mexican Americans born in the US necessarily resulted in an increase in the ethnic Mexican population's political activism.*

Was Garcia assuming that? Yes, it seems. That's why the author is pushing back against that assumption.

If the correct answer isn't testing that line (which seems like our best match for the question stem's keywords), then it will be reinforcing some other part of Garcia's worldview, as we've heard it described:
- the activism in the 30-60s was a precursor to that in the 60s under Chavez
- among the activists there was both vibrant diversity of thought and cooperative instincts based on shared goals
- Mexican Americans born in the U.S. and exposed to WWII wartime rhetoric were made to feel more like they were part of mainstream culture, more like they were entitled to the full complement of mainstream American rights, and more willing to agitate for those things.

choices.text: Increased ethnic consciousness among Mexican Americans accounted for an increase in political activity among them.
choices.explanation:
The author is thinking that ****decreased**** ethnic consciousness accounted for an increase in political activity, if we imagine that it's a zero sum game between acculturating to the U.S. and maintaining the ethnic culture from Mexico.

Garcia thinks that these activists were a new generation of leaders,
*one that was more acculturated and* *****hence***** *more politically active than its predecessor.*

choices.text: Increased familiarity among Mexican Americans with United States culture accounted for an increase in political activity among them.
choices.explanation:
In the second sentence of the final paragraph, the author says that Garcia argues that a new generation of Mexican American leaders appeared.

They were more acculturated. Hence, they were more politically active.

Assumption? *Being more acculturated made them more politically active*.

choices.text: The assimilation of many Mexican Americans into United States culture accounted for Mexican Americans' lack of interest in political activity.
choices.explanation:
Being assimilated = being acculturated

As we've discussed in (A) and (B), the author believes that assimilating more into US culture, absorbing the wartime rhetoric, and becoming resolved to achieve full civil rights were all motivating Mexican Americans to have ****more**** interest in political activity.

choices.text: Many Mexican Americans were moved to political militancy as a means of achieving full civil rights for all United States residents of Mexican descent.
choices.explanation:
The term "militant" is a strong one, meaning "radical, inflexible, maximalist, dogmatic". A *militant* vegan is one who won't eat of any grill that has ever been used to cook meat and who makes all the people they're eating with feel guilty about any animal products they're consuming.

In this passage, *militant* is only used in the first paragraph, to describe the activists in the 1960s.

choices.text: Many Mexican Americans were moved to political protest by their experience of discrimination and the patronizing rhetoric of World War II slogans.
choices.explanation:
"Patronizing" means to look down on someone, to condescend.

The passage identifies the wartime rhetoric as *inclusive*, as in "You're our equal! Let's all pitch in as fellow Americans of all backgrounds to stop Hitler."

questions.prompt: It can be inferred that the author of the passage believes which one of the following about the Mexican American political activists of the 1930s and 1940s?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
The author mentions the 19330s and 40s in the first paragraph, saying she is convinced by Garcia that these activists anticipated many of the reforms proposed by the more militant Chicanos of the 1960s and 70s.

So the author believes:
- they were less militant than activists that came later
- they foreshadowed / laid the groundwork for eventual reforms that came later

However, the author's *Opinion* of these earlier activists also comes through as the author talks about the two big flaws she sees in Garcia's study.

In the 2nd paragraph, our author is stressing that there was a lot of tension and conflict between different factions of activists at the time (one group was often diametrically opposed to another).

In the 3rd paragraph, our author is just saying is a very wispy, noncommittal way that it's possible that the greater determination to achieve full civil rights was something possessed mainly by activists and not as much by other Mexican Americans of the same era.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
Let's look for something safely worded that aligns with
- less militant than later activists
- foreshadowed / laid groundwork for later reforms
- fought a lot with each other
- may have been way more committed to achieving full civil rights than were there non-activist contemporaries.

choices.text: Their common goal of liberal reform made them less militant than the Mexican American activists of the 1960s and 1970s.
choices.explanation:
This answer sort of puts the opposite of the 3rd idea into a causal connection with the 1st idea
**- less militant than later activists**
- foreshadowed / laid groundwork for later reforms
**- fought a lot with each other**
- may have been way more committed to achieving full civil rights than were there non-activist contemporaries.

We know the author thinks the activists from the 30s/40s were less militant, but she never says it's **because** of the activists in the 30s/40s (unlike in the 60s/70s?) had the common goal of liberal reform.

choices.text: Their common goal of liberal reform did not outweigh their political differences.
choices.explanation:
This answer is expressing the author's main point in the 2nd paragraph, the 3rd of our possible answer ideas:

**- less militant than later activists**
- foreshadowed / laid groundwork for later reforms
**- fought a lot with each other**
- may have been way more committed to achieving full civil rights than were there non-activist contemporaries.

The author takes issue with Garcia for "acknowledging these [stark] differences between different activist groups but *dismissing them as insignificant*, given that the goals of all the groups centered on liberal reform."

The following sentence starts with a Pivot, where the author pushes back. "**But** ... [even though they had a common goal of liberal reform] one need only note the fierce controversies that occurred during X to recognize that Mexican American history since 1930 has been characterized by intense and lively debate".

choices.text: Their common goal of liberal reform helped them reach a consensus in spite of their political differences.
choices.explanation:
This answer is basically the opposite of (B).

This answer would better reflect Garcia's position, that even though these activists had their differences, they were united under the common goal of liberal reform.

This answer seems to go against our 3rd idea.

**- less militant than later activists**
- foreshadowed / laid groundwork for later reforms
**- fought a lot with each other**
- may have been way more committed to achieving full civil rights than were there non-activist contemporaries.

choices.text: They were more or less evenly divided between those favoring assimilation and those favoring cultural maintenance.
choices.explanation:
Nothing in the passage speaks to a quantified comparison between the activists that favor assimilation and those that favor cultural maintenance.

The author seemed more to be suggesting that "although the activists were more in favor of assimilation, the rest of the Mexican American population was more into favoring cultural maintenance."

choices.text: They did not succeed in fully achieving their political goals because of their disparate political views.
choices.explanation:
This answer sort of puts the 2nd idea into a causal connection with the 3rd idea.

**- less militant than later activists**
**- foreshadowed / laid groundwork for later reforms**
**- fought a lot with each other**
- may have been way more committed to achieving full civil rights than were there non-activist contemporaries.

We know that the activists had disparate political views. We never hear specifically about whether they fully achieved their goals. We can probably assume that they didn't *fully* achieve their goals if they anticipated reforms that came later. Plus, who in life ever really *fully* achieves their goals? That seems like a very safe expression to sign off on.

However, there's just no textual support for any causal connection between "disparate views" and "failing to fully achieve goals".

questions.prompt: The author of the passage expresses uncertainty with regard to which one of the following?

explanationBlocks.heading: Support Window
explanationBlocks.body:
Where do we see the author expressing uncertainty? We'd check any of paragraphs 2 or 3, where the author's voice is frequently present.

The sentence that begins "However" sounds like it's expressing uncertainty.

The author is uncertain whether the determination of Mexican American activists in the 30s-60s (to achieve full civil rights and continue assimilating into mainstream US culture) was shared by more regular Mexican Americans who may have had more of their traditional Mexican ethnic consciousness, depending on whether they only spoke Spanish and depending on how fast they could immigrate into the US and be naturalized.

choices.text: whether or not one can assume that the increase in the number of Mexican Americans born in the United States led to an increase in Mexican American political activism
choices.explanation: In the last sentence the author definitively says we ****cannot**** assume this.

choices.text: whether or not historians preceding Garcia were correct in their assumptions about Mexican Americans who were politically active between 1930 and 1960
choices.explanation: The historians preceding Garcia are obliquely mentioned in the first paragraph, but we aren't told any of their assumptions about Mexican Americans' political activity in the 30s-60s.

choices.text: whether or not there was general consensus among Mexican American political activists between 1930 and 1960
choices.explanation: The last sentence of the second paragraph establishes that this group of activists were characterized "****not**** by consensus, but by intense and lively debate".

choices.text: the extent to which the views of Mexican American activists were shared by the ethnic Mexican population in the United States
choices.explanation:
This lines up nicely with our Support Window.

We found the best line reference for "author's uncertainty":
*However,* *****it is not clear***** *how far this outlook extended*

And this answer just says what that sentence says -- the author isn't sure whether the political activism exhibited by the activists was shared by regular old Mexican Americans or if it was an anomaly.

choices.text: the nature of the relationship between the League of United Latin American Citizens and the Congress of Spanish-Speaking People
choices.explanation:
This is nowhere near our Support Window towards the end of the 3rd paragraph. This comes from the middle of the 2nd paragraph. The author doesn't seem uncertain about the relationship.

She says the former group was often "diametrically opposed to" the latter group.

questions.prompt: The passage supports which one of the following statements about ethnic consciousness among Mexican Americans?

explanationBlocks.heading: Supporting Text
explanationBlocks.body:
We're looking for where the passage talks about "ethnic consciousness", or awareness of one's ethnicity.

It shows up in the final sentence (which is like 10 lines long!)

The sentence right before it is saying, "However, it is not clear *whether the political activism of Mexican American leaders striving for full civil rights for US residents of Mexican descent* was actually representative of that broader generation of Mexican Americans."

"Ethnic consciousness" is brought up as a potential variable that would make the average Mexican American pretty different from these Mexican American activist leaders.

The passage is suggesting that there were some Mexican Americans who were already bilingual and naturalized and feeling like Americans and thus agitating for their rights as fully participatory Americans, and that meanwhile there were more recently immigrated, not-yet-naturalized, not-yet-bilingual Mexican Americans who were way more Mexican than American in their hearts.

They were still steeped in the ethnic consciousness of being a Mexican who happens to now live in America, unlike the activists who saw themselves primarily as Americans who happen to have Mexican descent.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: We know that ethnic consciousness was thought to vary significantly enough in this generation of Mexican Americans that the author believes that the political activism of some of them would not be shared to the same degree by others.

choices.text: Ethnic consciousness increases when rates of Mexican immigration and naturalization increase.
choices.explanation: The author doesn't clarify a specific relationship here. The author is saying that variables like immigration and naturalization rates help to create variables in ethnic consciousness, but we can't tell whether it's a positive relationship or an inverse one.

choices.text: Ethnic consciousness increases when the number of Mexican Americans born in the United States increases.
choices.explanation: The author doesn't clarify a specific relationship here. The author is saying that you can't assume that as the number of MA's born in the US increases that MA's political activism will increase. But we don't have a direct link from political activism to ethnic consciousness.

choices.text: Ethnic consciousness decreases when the number of Mexican Americans assimilating into the culture of the United States increases.
choices.explanation:
The author doesn't clarify a specific relationship here. This answer sounds like a highly plausible one, but we can't find any line reference to support it.

Ethnic consciousness is brought up in a very wishy-washy way, sort of just suggesting that its variability makes for messy inferences. Yet these first three answers all tried to create a very clean inference with ethnic consciousness that we just don't have any explicit support for.

choices.text: Variations in the influence of Mexican American leaders over the Mexican American population at large account in part for variations in ethnic consciousness.
choices.explanation: The author only indicates that "variables such as patterns of bilingualism and rates of immigration and naturalization" create variation in ethnic consciousness. The passage doesn't connect variations in ethnic consciousness to variations in the influence of Mex-American leaders.

choices.text: Variations in rates of Mexican immigration and naturalization account in part for variations in ethnic consciousness.
choices.explanation:
That final sentence indicates that "****variables**** such as patterns of bilingualism and rates of immigration and naturalization" create variation in ethnic consciousness.

*the variations in ethnic consciousness* *****these variables***** *help to create*
